subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF TASK FORCE ON LABOUR-MANAGEMENT LAW

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF TASK FORCE ON LABOUR-MANAGEMENT LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table the progress report prepared by the task force on labour relations that some days ago the Prime Minister assured the house would be tabled at an early date. This report indicates that the task force is well advanced in a thorough examination of industrial relations policies, problems and practices.
An extensive and important program of basic studies is outlined in an appendix to the report. These studies and the discussions
being held with union, employer and government groups in all parts of the country will undoubtedly assist the task force in dealing with the major issues set forth in this initial report, including special problems which may arise in the case of disputes in essential industries. The task force has undertaken to complete its work by the end of this year.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the tabling of this report by the government is not to be regarded as establishing a precedent. There will no doubt be occasions in the future when the government may decide not to table reports of task forces. A major purpose of the work of such special consultants frequently is to provide advice on the formulation of government policy, and it is the policy itself, decided upon after full consideration of the advice available to it, which a government must, of course, make clear to the house and the country as a whole. In some circumstances, however, it will also be desirable, in the interests of greater public awareness and understanding of complex issues, to make public the texts of reports by the task forces or other consultants. Hence the tabling of this report, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF TASK FORCE ON LABOUR-MANAGEMENT LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tabling of the report at this time is, I suggest, a somewhat curious step. Perhaps it is meant to bring about some retroactive or advanced blessing for the promise of the Prime Minister a year ago that this report would be before us prior to the introduction of major legislation in the field of labour.
Until we have seen the report we will not know how much it impinges on Bill No. C-186, the very controversial measure that is now being studied by a house committee. However, in his brief statement the minister did refer to the fact that the report dealt with disputes in essential industries, and this is one of the problems that has bothered members of that particular committee in the issue it is facing. We will withhold further judgment on the report until it is studied, but I think it is regrettable that the final study, not just an interim study, was not before us prior to the introduction of the measure of the house.

February 29, 1968

I had assumed that it was a precedent, because another report in the field of foreign ownership was tabled the other day. subtopic: MEASURE TO BROADEN COVERAGE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen (for Mr. Nicholson) for the second reading of Bill No. C-197, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.

subtopic: MEASURE TO BROADEN COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the regulations under the act were amended by order in council in 1957 to bring fishermen within the purview of the Unemployment Insurance Act and provide them with coverage, the then minister of labour, Milton Gregg, admitted that this action was taken in order to establish a sort of welfare scheme for fishermen to meet economic difficulties at that time prevailing in the Atlantic provinces. In fact, this coverage is still looked upon by many as a sort of welfare scheme.
The minister of fisheries of that day, Jimmy Sinclair, when this matter was dealt with in 1957, also stated on a number of occasions that this step brought about a regulatory monstrosity, that anybody who looked at the regulations would realize that the act and its concept had been distorted to provide coverage for fishermen. The difficulty that arose was in trying to assist people who found it difficult to obtain regular employment for a reasonable period of time, and grafting that
Unemployment Insurance Act concept on to another concept. As a consequence the regulations relating to fishermen are most inequitable in their application.
Primarily the regulations provide that a fisherman becomes entitled to seasonal benefits and is required to contribute to the fund for 15 weeks to become eligible. However, I am sure that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), coming as he does from British Columbia, knows quite well that some of the "high line" fishermen, as we call them, do make a fairly good income from fishing, at least by fishermen's standards. In some cases, to pick a figure out of the air, they make $9,000 or $10,000. Yet even with such incomes they are eligible to receive unemployment insurance benefits after they have made their 15 weekly contributions.
These "high line" fishermen look upon these unemployment benefits as nothing more than beer money, and they are commonly referred to as such among fishermen. On the other hand, the man who is a gill net fisherman sometimes finds his opportunities to fish restricted by Department of Fisheries closures, and thus he may be denied the opportunity of earning a living for some weeks during the fishing season. Consequently his income during the season may amount to a paltry couple of thousand dollars, and at the end of the fishing season he finds himself in debt to the fishing company. Thus the fisherman who most needs assistance is discriminated against because he is unable to put in his 15 weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. In many cases this is because the colleague of the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robi-chaud), has denied this fisherman the opportunity to fish as a result of the imposition of closures for conservation purposes.
I am not questioning the value of closures. I believe we must concern ourselves about conservation. However, it is an anomaly when regulations permit someone with a fairly substantial income to draw unemployment insurance benefits which are looked upon as pin money but at the same time deny similar payments to fishermen who really need them. I say this principle is wrong and has been so ever since 1957. Everyone in the fishing industry knows it is wrong and I am sure the minister knows it is wrong. Yet the regulation in question is still in existence. It should have been changed years ago and it should be changed now.
It seems passing strange, Mr. Speaker, in view of the extensive study that was obviously made of unemployment insurance on behalf
February 29. 1968
Unemployment Insurance Act of the government by the Gill committee more than five years ago, that such an anomaly has not been removed from the legislation. The regulations have to take into account the peculiarities of the fishing industry. For example, the employer-employee relationship is different from that in most other industries; it is not so direct or well connected. That they do so is reflected by the fact that they are extremely involved and intricate. Therefore, because of these peculiarities and the different concept involved it seems to me that the regulations should be altered once more so as to gear them to the need of fishermen for unemployment insurance benefits, which is directly related to the amount of income at their disposal. If their income is obviously low, they need assistance; if it is high they do not. I think that this misuse of the concept that people in difficult circumstances require assistance should be removed.
I should now like to pass on to another section of the act. Many times in this house questions have been asked about section 54 and the deprivation of benefits as a result of a strict interpretation of whether or not employment is available for certain people. I shall read briefly from the act in order that the section to which I refer will appear in the context of my comments. Section 54(2) reads as follows:
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
An insured person is disqualified from receiving benefit in respect of every day for which he fails to prove that he was
(a)	capable of and available for work, and
(b)	unable to obtain suitable employment.
The words "available for work" need to be dealt with. The minister knows this. The matter has been raised by many members of the house on a number of occasions. I think I am right in saying that the minister's predecessor, now the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), agreed in essence with the complaints and strictures concerning the part I read. He intended to do something about it but the language is still there. Difficulties have continued for years, and I submit this is all wrong.
I know of instances where insurance officers by means of leading questions to applicants for unemployment insurance benefits have disqualified those applicants. In Terrace, British Columbia, a woman who had worked in a hospital went before an insurance officer who asked her questions along these lines. person was deliberately led into the position of being disqualified but I believe that certain questions directed to her may have been responsible for her disqualification. When this lady went to register for unemployment insurance she was notified that she was disqualified because she had restricted herself so far as employment was concerned. I believe there is a need for better public relations between those who administer the Unemployment Insurance Act and the people who contribute to the unemployment insurance fund. Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss in failing to take part in this debate, because having been unemployed myself more than once, I am quite familiar with the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act and with the problems which arise at times. I would also
Unemployment Insurance Act be remiss in not calling the attention of the house to certain facts which, in my opinion, should be corrected.
First of all, I must say I am in favour of this bill designed to readjust benefit rates. But it must nevertheless be admitted that this piece of legislation contains certain restrictions, as evidenced by three things. It involves something "contradictory" "compulsory" and "contributory."
What I find strange and wish to stress at once is the contradiction apparent in the bill. An increasing number of people are in favour of full employment and believe this possible. They try therefore to improve the Unemployment Insurance Act. I must point out right away this obvious contradiction. They should be honest enough to admit that full employment is practically impossible in a period of rapid development, when working methods are changed by automation, with the result that a certain percentage of workers are always out of work. Railway workers know something about it, and it is unfortunate that the expected and vaguely promised adjustment of benefits has been delayed so long.
You will agree that I could also mention many other classes of workers.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
However, let us rather try to be logical in the face of the existing situation, and let us consider how the workers suffering from unemployment could be helped.
Since the passing of the Unemployment Insurance Act, more than twenty-five years ago, a number of changes have been made. In the majority of cases, it was mostly a matter of trying to secure the protection of the fund and providing employment for a growing number of government employees.
In 1942, the government's contributions and the dues paid by employers and employees were about $44 million and administration costs a little over $2 million, while unemployed workers received $27,752,000 in benefits.
And in 1962, twenty years later, the amount of contributions by government, employers and employees was a little over $325 million, the benefits paid were over $400 million with $45 million in administration costs. This is now big business, and a lot of money changes hands.
The proposed amendments to Bill No. C-197 are socialistic in spirit: to extend coverage of the Unemployment Insurance Act to all

February 29, 1968

Unemployment Insurance Act Canadians with a yearly income of up to $7,800. The government wants to include as many people as possible in the compulsory contribution system.
There is nothing in Bill No. C-197 providing for changes to be made in the established methods of making more flexible the eligibility requirements of an unemployed worker. The protection of the fund is first provided for.
The rate of benefits shall increase in proportion to the gains made by the worker. Salaries, in many regions called economically underprivileged areas, are generally low. The increase in benefits will not therefore be proportional to the increase in the cost of living.
I am not against an adjustment in the rates of dues, benefits and non deducted gains. However, one must not forget that the principal aim of an unemployment insurance act is to help the unemployed. Noting that those who prepared Bill No. C-197 seem to have taken great pains to protect the fund rather than the unemployed, I conclude that this protective spirit will reveal itself especially through the inspectors of the commission who are often inclined to take a chance on spending $100 in an attempt to find that a poverty stricken unemployed has received $5 or $10 too much in benefits.
To my mind, the most important thing the government should do, first of all, instead of paralysing construction through higher interest rates and taxes on building materials, is to undertake vast construction programs and build hospitals, old peoples' homes, rehabilitation centres for the handicapped of all ages and research centres.
The implementation of such programs would contribute to reducing unemployment and would be more in order than the introduction of medicare which will not give the people of this country one single additional doctor or hospital bed. How many other useful projects could be undertaken to reduce considerably the effects of that social evil which is called unemployment. Whether it be occasional, fractional, seasonal or chronic-those are the new words we have found since the act was passed in 1946-an unemployment period is always demoralizing for its victims.
That is why we should have an act, clearly drafted, with rules to enable understanding civil servants-I know there are some, I know many of them-to really help the unemployed through a humane application of a so-called social law.

High officials, civil servants, at middle or lower echelons, would do well to remember that they are the servants of the people and not their tyrants, that the people are individuals and not robots; in short, that the people pay them and that they expect from them services and not trouble.
A better act might keep them from evading the law of gravity, and let them keep both feet on the ground as well as keep them from getting swelled heads, which at times leads some of them to think too highly of themselves, with the result that the unemployed experience serious difficulties.

Now, the unemployment insurance officer, who has not examined the worker- it is exactly what I am saying in this notice of appeal to the board of referees-decided that the worker is unavailable for work, unable to do the work that should be done at this time of the year. The strange thing about it all is that, at this period of the year, the officers know very well that this seasonal worker, a lumberman, has no work available because all operations in the bush are finished everywhere for the season. Here is proof that the officers are overzealous in trying to deprive a lumberman of unemployment insurance benefits by offering him a possible or probable job in the bush.
I remember that four or five years ago, payment of benefits had been suspended for close to 300 workers in the Kamouraska riding and a good many in Temiscouata, in fact up to Rimouski. It almost created a scandal. Why? Because a high official of the commission had come at one time to the Riviere-du-Loup office and had felt that there were too many unemployed in the district.
It is not the people's fault that they live in an economically underprivileged area. It is not necessary for an official to leave the Montreal office and try to penalize all those who are having unemployment trouble. Of course, that situation has been settled; but I have seen government employees working nights to find the names and addresses of unemployed workers and sending them employment offers. Then they had to work nights too in order to pay those people their benefits, for the official's decision had obviously fallen through. We met a high official of the Department of Labour, who was the chief commissioner of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. He understood the problem and the matter was settled advantageously. But why let these workers suffer a

month because they have problems due to lack of income, because they were unemployed?
Mr. Speaker, I now conclude my remarks because I did not want to speak too long on the subject since I am anxious, like most hon. members, to see this bill passed. However, I cannot resume my seat without stressing a particular point which quite impressed me.
In passing, I wish to mention at once that even if I come from the Kamouraska area, this does not mean necessarily that the examples which I give bear the signature of the officials in the offices of my area. Not at all. There are officials in the Montreal offices and in many areas. Having been in contact with workers right across the province for ten years, from 1952 to 1962, I happen to receive correspondence from almost everywhere.
I shall not mention the place where this letter came from, but the fact remains that it was written by an official on a letterhead of the commission following a decision of the board of referees. The official in question had rendered a decision by which the unemployed who was awaiting benefits was disqualified. However, the unemployed, faced with his problems, appealed to the board of referees where his situation was discussed. In its conclusion, the board says this.
It is absolutely disgusting. One would never think that people could say such things, but to write them, on top of that!
During their discussions, the members of the board of referees recognize that the reason why this man stopped working may be a valid one from the human point of view, but not in the eyes of the law, since it is considered to be a personal reason. That is why they have no alternative but to uphold the decision of the unemployment insurance office and reject the appeal.
I would suggest to the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) that he should be careful in choosing officials who have to make decisions. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, there are very good, highly competent and understanding officials-I know some. On the other hand, I know others who are not qualified to do the work they do and who come to conclusions that are very unfavourable to an unemployed man who has to contend with poverty. Those are the ones that should be watched.

Until now it has been possible for Indian and Eskimo employees in our labour force not to be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. Two matters relating to the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act as it affects northern Canada should be brought before the minister. One of them has to do with the regulations. In so many words they say that any person employed north of the sixtieth parallel of latitude whose livelihood is not ordinarily derived from insurable employment shall not necessarily be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. This provision was first brought in around 1959, the intention being to encourage private concerns to employ Indians and Eskimos. But the provision has fulfilled its purpose and its effect now is to bring about, if I may term it this way, discrimination in reverse.
Construction companies which move to northern Canada for summer operations bring part of their labour force with them from the cities in the south but they will also hire some semi-skilled people locally. Most of these are hunters or trappers who because of their construction skills are hired by the construction companies. Sometimes they have jobs for six, eight, ten or 12 months at any one time. The point is that though they may be eligible for benefits their employers are taking advantage of that part of the regulations to which I referred. I ask the minister to take a hard look at those regulations to see if their purpose has not been fulfilled. I think we should give our Indian and Eskimo residents full benefits under this act just as if they lived south of the sixtieth parallel.
Another point deserves the minister's attention. Some hon. members speak of unemployment insurance offices being 150 miles from

certain towns. The unemployment insurance office closest to the sixtieth parallel is at Edmonton, about 450 miles away. If you go as far north as Inuvik you are talking about 1,300 or 1,400 miles. There may be an argument that not enough people live there to justify an office but I believe other factors ought to be considered. If we are to encourage private development in northern Canada the services of government must be available to private entrepreneurs as they would be in southern Canada. Inuvik is a long way from Edmonton. Granted, the mail service is reasonable but there is the question of dialogue to consider. It would be better for our people if an officer of the commission could be stationed in the capital of the Northwest Territories, Yellowknife. He would be in a good position to deal with the particular and peculiar problems which arise when private entrepreneurs operate in the north.
Another reason for having an officer there is that situations similar to the one in 1964 might arise again. One of our major mines in Yellowknife had a fire in the head frame which resulted in the mine and the mill having to be closed down for three or four months. Had it not been for the initiative of the local people, benefits might have been delayed more than they were.
The commission provides reasonable service in the northern part of Canada but it would help us to have an unemployment insurance office established there. Mr. Speaker, first I would like to thank all hon. members, who have contributed to this debate. Some very helpful and constructive suggestions have been made for improvement in the administration of the unemployment insurance program generally and I am happy to inform all hon. members through you, Mr. Speaker, if they do not already know it, that the chief commissioner of the unemployment commission and other officials have been in the gallery throughout the whole of the debate and they have had the benefit of hearing all the suggestions made by hon. members.
I might say that I am gratified, although not surprised, that all parties and groups in the house have signified approval in principle of the amendments contained in the bill. However, a great many members have expressed regret that the bill does not go farther and include more of the recommendations that were contained in the report of the Gill committee which completed its work some five years ago. In reply, I would point out that the recommendations of the Gill committee were very comprehensive, but hon. members will recall that they were made at a time of serious unemployment in Canada when the funds of the Unemployment Insurance Commission were exhausted. Those funds had to be replenished through special votes by the house on two different occasions. I am glad to say that conditions have changed since then, and while some of the recommendations of the Gill committee merit implementation, others require at least modification.
As has been stated on previous occasions in this house, the Gill committee report was referred some time ago to an interdepartmental committee. The government has had an interim report from that committee and the committee has been asked to study it further.
Unemployment Insurance Act I would like to inform hon. members that a comprehensive revision of this act, to include 50 per cent or maybe more of the recommendations made by the Gill committee, and the modified recommendations that may come out of the study being made by the interdepartmental committee, would involve months of study in this house. It would not be a simple piece of legislation. I am convinced it would require a minimum of three months study by this house, and probably much longer.
When the government was faced with this situation, realizing that there had been no change made to the act for a period of some nine years and that the scale of benefits is not realistic in view of the changes that have taken place in the economy over the last four or five years, it was our opinion that there could be no further delay and that at the least we would have to introduce without delay the amendments covered in this bill. I particularly felt a responsibility because on more than one occasion during the past 12 months I had assured hon. members that in this session of parliament I would introduce amendments along the lines covered in this bill now before us. That accounts for the fact that we have a relatively short, simple bill to take care of immediate requirements, with the assurance on the part of the government that a more detailed, a more comprehensive bill, an overhaul bill, if you want to so describe it, will be introduced at the earliest possible date.
Hon. members, who have expressed support in principle for the bill, have also raised some very interesting questions which I think call for brief comment on my part at this stage. For instance, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) referred to some calculations based on a table contained in clause 4 of the bill. The proportion of the benefit for persons with dependants has been maintained at 50 per cent or more of the new table which will apply when amendments to the act come into effect. This is in keeping with accepted unemployment insurance practice in many countries of the world including our neighbour to the south. Because it is included by them is no reason that we should accept it, but at least it is an indication that we are moving in ways which other countries consider to be fair and reasonable.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) requested certain information which I am pleased to furnish. He asked for statistics concerning the status of the fund at the present time. I am happy to report that as of the end of the last fiscal year, March 31, 1967, the unemployment insurance fund had a credit of about $258 million. This is quite different from the situation we had a few years ago when it was necessary to replenish the fund in the period 1962 and 1963, the first two years that I was in this house. We can only estimate the condition of the fund at the end of this present fiscal year, since unemployment usually runs higher during the months of November through March. Five of these months are behind us, however, and present indications are that the fund will be just in excess of $300 million at the end of this fiscal year.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Ry-nard), the hon. member for Kings (Mr. McQuaid), the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and also one of the last speakers, the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Pascoe), all referred to the closing of some unemployment insurance offices. I believe that there has been some misunderstanding about this. Perhaps a little information on this subject might be helpful, not so much for members but for the information of the general public.

When the Unemployment Insurance Commission was first established the responsibility for the administration of the national employment service was delegated to the commission. The commission continued to perform that function until after the report of the Glassco royal commission was published. The Glassco commission studied the workings of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and felt that there was a conflict of interest between the national employment service and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In its report the Glassco commission recommended that these two services be separated.
I was a member of an ad hoc cabinet committee which studied the recommendations of the Glassco commission and, if my memory serves me right, we recommended that this and several other recommendations contained in the Glassco commission report be implemented. As a result, at the beginning of the fiscal year, April 1, 1965, the two functions were separated. This was not done at the time the Department of Manpower and Immigration came into existence in December, 1965. It had been done some nine months earlier. As a result much of the work and the necessity for much of the staff in the unemployment insurance offices disappeared when this function was turned over to another branch of the government.
At the same time the commission, which is charged with the responsibility of administering this act efficiently and economically in the national interest, realized that a great advantage would accrue from the use of computers and other modern systems. The two were synchronized. There has been a closing of certain offices but there are manpower offices in most of these areas and there are officials of government who can furnish information to people who make application under the Unemployment Insurance Act and its regulations and they are happy to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I will defer to the sponsor of the bill if he wishes to make some comments. However, he has not risen

and we do not want to get into the same predicament as we did on the last bill. I have a few words to say on this bill. Before the consideration of the bill goes beyond the committee stage I should like assurance from the sponsor of the bill that Bill C-231, the National Transportation Act, passed by this house has been proclaimed. I am under the impression that the section dealing with commodity pipe lines was exempted from the proclamation. This, of course, leaves us in a very poor position. It leaves us in the position of creating a commodity pipe line-this, of course, will be the first one of its kind to handle solids in Canada-without any legislation under which its operations can be supervised.
A great deal of discussion of this commodity pipe line has taken place. I have had the opportunity of discussing this bill with company officials on a number of occasions. I am convinced that the company is sincerely interested in developing not only a research proposition but a commodity pipe line that will handle a product as soon as the pipe line can be made operative.
One of the reasons for discussing the problems connected with solids pipe lines designed to handle basic raw materials was that in fact we were creating a new form of transportation. I do not know what the former minister of transport, now the chairman of the transportation commission, had in mind when he excluded part II of the act from the proclamation. I am sure the government did not exclude that part but that it was the chairman who decided that section would not be put into effect. Certainly he was aware of the purpose of including the solids pipe line section. I am sure he was aware of the need for protection of the consumers of this nation who are using transportation facilities.
We have been told how many thousands of box cars will be taken off the railroads as a result of the construction of a pipe line that will handle basic commodities which are now shipped by rail. I understand this new form of transportation will reduce the price of the product considerably and will put the Shell Oil Company into a position to compete effectively in world markets. This is very worth while. If potash, sulphur and some of the other basic commodities can be carried to the west coast by this new form of transportation we will find that because of the decreased use of rail and highway transportation there will be a change in the cost of the freight that will continue to be handled by the railways and over the highways. It is essential so far as I 27053-4491

am concerned, therefore, that part III of the National Transportation Act be proclaimed before this pipe line is constructed.
My recent discussions with company officials indicate they are convinced they have overcome the problems that were involved in putting sulphur in an oil-based slurry to ship to the coast. They are of the opinion that they have been able to solve the problem of refining and removing the commodity from the oil base. Company officials have suggested they will make a number of amendments and I am told the amendments they will put into effect are worth while. In talking to their lawyers I was surprised that they were willing to take out of the bill some of the things I believe are absolutely necessary. We have agreed with the company that these things should be retained because this company will have immediate use for some of them. It seems to me it is no longer our responsibility to insist that certain protection be provided to the nation. The government should proclaim part II of the National Transportation Act which to my knowledge has not been proclaimed. No legitimate reason has been given for not proclaiming that part of the act.
In the transportation of a commodity such as sulphur the difficulties that accrue are many and the research requirements for the economic handling of this commodity are very great. It has been necessary for the company, through research, to arrive at a specific gravity for the sulphur that will allow the company to put the product through the pipe line in a volume equal to about 80 per cent of the total volume of the line. The specific gravity of the product going through the line has to be close enough to the specific gravity of the carrier to enable the company to get the slurry moving again following an emergency shutdown. Otherwise, of course, the solids would remain in the pipe line and a great deal of difficulty would be created.
I have had conversations with other pipe line officials and I find there are a number of ways of handling solids. We were told that commodities such as sulphur might have to be transported in capsule form. Some research has been done into the transportation of sulphur in round or oblong blocks. If for some reason the carriage of these balls of sulphur breaks down, say as a result of pumping difficulties, the specific gravity of the sulphur, being the same as the air in the line, would permit a bottleneck to be avoided.

Anyone who has had anything to do with sulphur knows that it comes in different forms. The pipe line, therefore, will be governed by the commodity pipe line section of the transport bill. Is that right?

Yes. It certainly will be, under part II, but I have already put on the record what the Minister of Transport has authorized me to say, that part II will be proclaimed before anyone starts building a solids pipe line. Part II has not been proclaimed because the regulations have not been drawn up. The point I was making is that even though part II has not been proclaimed, as the hon. member knows, a proposal to carry hydrocarbons is at the present time governed by the National Energy Board Act. Since an oil base will be used to carry the sulphur the pipe line cannot operate without an application to the National Energy Board first being made.
As the hon. member knows, when dealing with a commodity pipe line which uses a hydrocarbon carrier, a combined application must be made to the National Energy Board and to the Canadian Transport Commission. My point is that though part II has not yet been proclaimed it will be, and it will cover this pipe line.
Because of the undertaking I have put on record and because the National Energy Board is involved in the matter, I hope the hon. member is satisfied. His objections were legitimate. This
measure has been before us on a number of occasions. There has been a considerable difference of opinion as to whether or not it is a Canadian company. We have from time to time been concerned about the number of insurance companies which have made petitions to parliament. When this particular bill was introduced, the impression was given that it was a Canadian-owned company. The sponsor confused the issue in his opening remarks on November 2, 1967, when he said, as reported in Hansard at page 3814:
For the information of the hon. member this company is a Canadian company originally incorporated in Manitoba in 1906 and subsequently
February 29, 1968

Incorporated under Chapter 70 of the statutes of 1910. The original company, Eagle Star, was a British company.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
Although to the sponsor this is a Canadian company, the ownership of the company is totally foreign. As Mr. Humphrys said on January 23:
The British Northwestern Insurance Company is a federal company, having been federally incorporated in 1917, but it started earlier as a provincial company. It is owned by the Eagle Star Insurance Company, a prominent British company with world wide interests and a very large volume of business.
How does it become a Canadian company? If this is a Canadian company merely because it is incorporated in Canada, then we have no problem with any companies which are federally incorporated. Being incorporated here they would automatically be naturalized Canadian companies. But in my opinion, and I am sure I will be supported by every person who is interested in seeing Canadian control of Canadian industry, because this company is financed by British money it is not a Canadian owned company.
For some time we in this party have been concerned about the question of foreign owned companies. We have been urging that finance and insurance companies which apply for a federal charter should have a large percentage of Canadian ownership. It is not enough for us to say that we will not grant this company a charter because it will continue to do business under the name of Eagle Insurance. We are interested in seeing that it is made a good Canadian corporate citizen, the term used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. If companies are to become good corporate citizens it seems to me that a large part of the control over them should belong to Canadian citizens.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) has written a number of books on the subject of Canadians regaining control of the Canadian economy. The Watkins report, recently tabled under his auspices, points out a number of ways by which control of companies could pass into Canadian hands. Many persons have been interested in this subject, and numerous suggestions have been made. However, many insurance companies do not care about the matter. They do not care what relationship they have with their parent corporations. The return on their investment is more important to them than the actual method by which their companies are controlled.
Private Bills
I think it can safely be said that the Bell Telephone Company, with 2 per cent American ownership by American Bell, is just as dominated by American Bell as are other companies dominated by foreign parent corporations which control 50 per cent of their stock. I believe we should be working to develop Canadian ownership of all these companies, and in particular of insurance companies which collect moneys in Canada and can reinvest those moneys either in Canada or outside Canada.
If the theme of good corporate citizenship is developed fully, the majority of stock in a company must be owned by Canadian citizens. The Canadian public must have an opportunity to buy the stock of foreign subsidiaries. Other countries have taken steps in this direction. Not long ago the majority of companies in the Scandinavian countries were foreign owned, but then the governments of those countries took steps to buy into the foreign owned companies and stipulated that one seat on their boards of directors must be held by the government. As a result Sweden now owns a great percentage of its own industrial companies.
The Japanese passed a law stipulating that no foreigner could do business in Japan unless 51 per cent of the stock of his company was held by the government of Japan. Yet the Japanese are allowed to come to Canada where they are treated so generously and are given so many concessions that they may own 100 per cent of the corporations they establish here. Solutions for this problem can be found in the Watkins committee report, in the Gordon commission report of a few years ago, and in the reports of other commissions which have inquired into the subject.
Frankly I believe the problem is greatest in the insurance industry. That industry provides a lot of the money for capital investment in municipalities, for housing mortgages and in other fields which are important to the development of our nation. I have been shocked to read some reports of concessions that have been made to insurance companies to allow them to take out of the country the money they collect in Canada and invest it elsewhere.
Recently I was surprised to read an editorial in the Toronto Daily Star which referred to a cheap tax ride for Canada's insurance industry. It pointed out that the insurance industry draws 30 per cent of the personal savings of Canadians, and dealt with the reluctance of insurance companies to invest

their money in the industrial growth of the nation. It gave facts and figures which I hope some day to put on the record so that hon. members can consider them.
During consideration of a previous bill this session to incorporate the United Investment Life Assurance Company we made the suggestion that within two years of its commencing business it would sell 25 per cent of its stock to its officers, directors, or if necessary to other people who are Canadian residents. That company agreed to write into its charter that if within ten years it had not succeeded in selling 50 per cent of its shares to Canadian citizens, resident in Canada, it would give up its charter and dissolve. I think that company should be congratulated because it has said voluntarily that if it operates a Canadian company in a Canadian field it will be prepared to raise the money in Canada, sell the stock in Canada, and do business in Canada, and if it is not able to do that to the extent of 50 per cent in a period of ten years, it will give up its charter.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
I do not wish to put the sponsor of this bill on the spot by asking him to say that this company will accept the proposal that the United Investment Life Assurance Company was willing to accept. I shall not ask him to make a snap decision of this type today. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Germa):

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments in respect of Bill S-15, to incorporate Seaboard Finance Company of Canada. The Seaboard Finance Company of Canada is an Ontario incorporated company which seeks federal incorporation under the Small Loans Act. I believe it already is a known fact that this company engages in business throughout Canada under its provincial charter. So, should this company be granted federal incorporation, the only benefit that would accrue to it would be that it would have a little greater status in the community because the federal parliament had placed its hand upon it stating that it is free to go out in the business world to conduct the business of small loans.
The Seaboard Finance Company of Canada is a totally owned subsidiary of a large foreign investment company. The Prime Minister has stated that it is his belief and wish that Canadian industry and financial institutions should come progressively more and more under the jurisdiction of Canadian citizens. We believe this to be a good precedent. I should like to support the Prime Minister by saying that these companies which control large blocks of shares in our country should be under Canadian ownership and therefore responsive more to the needs of Canada and less to the needs and influences of a foreign country.
We are reluctant therefore to grant our blessing to this company, that it should go out into the world to conduct this business. Moneylenders have been with us since the beginning of time I presume. They are mentioned in the Bible. In the old days the moneylenders went into the temples and the high priests drove them with whips out of the temple. I do not propose that the moneylenders in this day and age should be whipped, but they certainly do not contribute to the well-being of our country when they charge usurious rates of interest to the people who are placed in the predicament of having to come into their clutches.
Under the Small Loans Act the Canadian people have borrowed approximately $900 million in order to acquire for themselves the
February 29, 19G8

things they need to carry on the business of living in Canada today. When we consider that the rate charged under the Small Loans Act sometimes is as high as 24 per cent we realize that a great deal of money which could otherwise be directed toward the production of more consumer goods is being siphoned off in the form of interest. If a greater percentage of this money which is paid out in the form of interest was retained as spending power in the hands of the consumers, I am sure more employment would be created. We would have a better standard of living and the whole economy of the nation would be improved if this money which is now being paid out in the form of usurious interest were left in the hands of the spender.

speechtext:
Before the house proceeded to the consideration of private bills, I heard the minister admit that there is need to improve the public relations of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and I am glad he said that. I assume the minister can assure the committee that no part of this bill, which is to amend the act, applies to school teachers in our schools and colleges. I note that the minister says it is impossible to have offices in every community in Canada. I submit that this government's centralization program is not providing a proper service to our people. We still ought to have unemployment insurance offices in every county of Ontario, as we had formerly. If we did that we could give our people far better service than they are now getting.
I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to comment briefly on Bill C-197, which is a bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. This indeed is a timely discussion because of the great amount of unemployment we now have in Canada. That rate has reached a high point of almost 7 per cent of the work force- and that rate contradicts the boasts of the various cabinet ministers about this country's great rate of economic progress.
Conditions are not as good in Canada as they might be. They are not as good as the government tries to make out they are. Under this government, all along the line production rates are falling, and often failing. This government does not look after our export trade as the previous government did. The annual increase in our gross national product this year stands at a new low. The export markets which were built up by the former Conservative government are being either lost or crippled as the result of the Kennedy round of trade agreements. That leads to unemployment. A leading example of the former statement, to do with export markets, is to be found in our diminishing wheat export sales.
I have in my hand a page from the Globe and Mail of February 28, and the heading over one article is, "Wheat exports sliding farther from '67 level". This proves that this government is not pursuing the promotion of wheat exports as vigorously as did the previous government. Lowering the level of exports certainly brings unemployment.
February 29, 1968
This country's canning and food processing industry, which is very important to my constituency of Prince Edward-Lennox, is not prospering as it should because this government's national and world outlook precludes it from giving that industry the assistance and service that is necessary for the industry to prosper. Accordingly we have more unemployment in our counties, in areas where fruit and food processing was a sustaining industry. These remarks tie in with unemployment and with the subject of this bill; that is because the policy of this government is creating more unemployment in the canning industry and other industries.
Evidently, from reading clause 1 of Bill C-197, the government foresees no change in our present high rate of unemployment. Those who earn up to $7,800 a year are to be brought under the act as insured persons. The government knows that those who earn between $5,460 and $7,800 per annum, and who are to be brought under this act, will no doubt have a better record of continuous employment than those who earn less. Therefore it is bolstering the unemployment insurance fund pretty much at the expense of this category of salaried persons. I also recognize that hourly wage rates have increased. These increases have put hourly wage earners into a position that is different from the one they occupied in the 1950's and early 1960's, so far as the application of the act is concerned. I cannot say that I support totally this new coverage nor that I support totally the new benefit rates. I caution the government to be careful about measures that make it more profitable for one to be unemployed.
In some quarters there is at present some uncertainty about the advisability of having compulsory unemployment insurance throughout the agricultural industry. I wish to place on record two resolutions from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which are contained in a brief they presented this week to the cabinet and to various parties in this house. The first resolution is headed "Declaration of Inconsiderable Employment". This, I take it, pertains to transient and seasonal labour, and it reads as follows:
Whereas certain segments of agricultural producers must rely on part time help; and
Whereas many of these part time employees are not interested in any other employment; and
Whereas it is unlikely that these employees would or could benefit from unemployment insurance;
Resolved that the Unemployment Insurance Commission reinstate the validity of the "Declaration of Inconsiderable Employment" so that part-time 27053-4501
Unemployment Insurance Act employees in agriculture have the prerogative as to whether they desire to be covered by Unemployment Insurance.
In other words, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is asking the government not to make the coverage of agricultural workers compulsory.
The next resolution in the brief reads as follows:
Whereas unemployment insurance was introduced for agricultural workers earlier in the year; and
Whereas the regulations were modified later in such a manner as to curtail its application to seasonal workers; and
Whereas the value or effect of Unemployment Insurance for farm labour is negligible;
Resolved that this program, as it applies to agriculture, be the subject of future study and recommendation by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
I recommend that the government's agricultural task force, which I assume is touring the country and looking into agricultural problems, consider these resolutions and conditions across the country and make recommendations regarding them.
I wish to bring up another point. Why is it so common for a man or woman who has paid unemployment insurance for many years, who has been a steady worker and never laid off, to have trouble collecting unemployment insurance when it is necessary to do so? Why are such people who have been steady workers and who have never been laid off so often refused cheques for extended periods? Why are they subject to humiliation and loss of money due to them, because of the runaround they so frequently get from the workers in the unemployment insurance offices? Why should these worthy insured persons be subject to the procrastination of clerks in these offices? Many instances of this have been brought to my attention, and in this connection I should like to quote from a letter I have received from a constituent calling attention, among other things, to the fact that people whose contributions have built up the very strength of the unemployment insurance fund cannot readily collect insurance when it is due to them, while on the other hand those who have been employed for only a short length of time, those whose employment record is never continuous, can usually walk into an unemployment insurance office and walk out with a cheque. I am sure I am not the only member of this house who has received complaints of this kind. This is one

February 29, 1968

Unemployment Insurance Act letter 1 received, under date of January 26, 1968:
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Dear Mr. Alkenbrack,
I am writing concerning unemployment insurance. I have worked almost continuously from the time I left high school and paid into unemployment all that time. I have never drawn unemployment before, until now. I was laid off on September 18, 1967 and had to correspond, back and forth for six weeks, before I finally got unemployment insurance.
So I have actually drawn a very short time and today I got a letter saying "We are waiting a decision on your claim. When received we will send any benefit that may be payable to you." I hardly think that's fair. After all you see people who only work long enough so they can draw, they go in and have no trouble at all getting insurance, while people who are willing to work keep them going. Then, when we get laid off, we have to put up an awful fight to get insurance.
My husband had the same trouble, he has worked for 15 years and this is only the second time he has ever drawn. He also had to wait for six weeks before he got anything. If it hadn't been for the small amount I drew, we would have starved to death. He never had a cent for six weeks. He had to phone over there-*
This letter is written by a lady in Picton, Ontario. When she refers to "over there" she is referring to the Belleville office. The letter continues:
He had to phone over there, write back and forth, and what all he didn't have to do. They also went through his book and took the lowest stamp and gave him $33 instead of $36. He worked for a trucking company and the majority of his stamps were the highest you pay. When I was getting something, we could at least eat and buy oil. Now we are beside ourselves with worry for you know as well as I that $33 does not even feed a family of six properly, let alone buy fuel, pay hydro and phone, make our house payment and pay any other bills that the average family has. Also, with that amount of money, we cannot afford doctor's coverage and hospitalization which is an added worry.
We will have to lose our house and all the hard work we put into it. Then what will we do? Our payment is smaller than most places to rent so if we can't pay it, how can we rent a place?
There are quite a few families in this area in the same predicament and I think its time somebody tried to help us or give us some idea how to help ourselves. There are parents and children in this town who are actually cold and hungry and most of them are good willing workers, but we just can't find any work. And the unemployment insurance think because we are from a small town they can pull the wool over our eyes and we'll sit back and take it.
That is all I shall read from that letter. I have visited this family. The lady is certainly not exaggerating. They are having a tough time; the money should have been available to them long ago. I am now investigating the above complaint and I know the minister will

give me every consideration because I am sure he will not tolerate this sort of treatment of applicants.
Here is another complaint from a constituent of mine in Napanee, a man who has been working for one firm all his life since 1913. How long ago is that, Mr. Chairman? Fifty five years, working for one firm, during which time he never drew an unemployment insurance benefit. I quote this letter to show the kind of ill treatment to which many people in this country are being subjected. The letter is dated February 15, 1968, and is as follows: Dear Sir,
In regard to unemployment I am sending this letter to you. As you know I have worked with the Napanee Iron Works, now the Napanee Industries, since 1913 at the age of 12 years, worked through two world wars.
I was ill in September 1966 and was home for some time. I was unable to return to the kind of work I had been doing. I had to have lighter work which they did not have at that time. The Napanee Industries gave me a lay-off slip until such time I applied for unemployment in September 1967 and was told by the manpower office in Kingston-
Here again I pause to inform the committee that the unemployment insurance office has been moved out of Napanee and centralized, in this case, in Kingston.
-that I did not have enough stamps in one year, also they wanted a doctor's certificate saying I was able to work, which I sent to them with a letter from Napanee Industries and the unemployment book with the stamps for my holiday pay for 1967. They still say I do not have enough stamps. I have paid unemployment since it started. It hardly seems fair. If there is anything that can be done about this I will really appreciate it.
Thanking you,
Milton Vanalstine.
I have no hesitation about reading this man's name into the record, because I have known him for years and I know he deserves whatever benefits the law will give him with regard to unemployment insurance. Canada owes this man and thousands more like him across our country a debt of gratitude, as well as the unemployment insurance which is coming to him after 55 years in the industrial service of this nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, both the minister and I are investigating this case. A good many of these evils and ills can be laid against the heartless practices and narrow confined thinking of bureaucracy. I am not entirely blaming this government. One must know and recognize the workings of bureaucracy. When these evils are pointed out to
February 29, 1968	COMMONS
whatever government happens to be in power I think that government should see to it that these wrongs are righted.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
We need a complete overhaul of the Unemployment Insurance Act to make it work in a more equitable way in serving unemployed people under present changing conditions, conditions unknown in the 1940's and 1950's. People who have contributed for many years should not be discriminated against. I find that the man who has never applied for unemployment insurance and has never drawn unemployment insurance benefits often disqualifies himself when filling out the tricky and intricate application forms. On the other hand, the man who goes often to an unemployment insurance office knows how to fill out these forms, so that thereby he does not disqualify himself.
As I have already inferred I want to impress upon the minister that I am very much against the moving of unemployment insurance offices to the larger centres. I am sure I speak for a large part of the country when I say this, because this is the general opinion across the country. This centralization is not good; it results in the power of decision being placed in the hands of officials who do not know local conditions. What does an official in Ottawa, Toronto, Kingston or Belleville know about the cases of local applicants in smaller centres like Napanee and Picton? I say to the government, quit recognizing the Unemployment Insurance Act and its benefits as a charity to be doled out in a niggardly manner to the people, and recognize the program for what it is: an insurance fund which belongs to the people who paid into it. They should have full and ready access to it in time of need.

subtopic: MEASURE TO BROADEN COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make that I hope will receive the minister's attention, and I also want to ask him a couple of questions. First, however, I wish to state that I am very glad that he has seen fit to exempt the teaching profession from compulsory contributions to the unemployment insurance fund. In the province from which I come there is absolutely no unemployment in the teaching profession, and there is not any chance that there will be unemployment in it.
There is one other profession that is in the same boat. I am sure the minister has
DEBATES	7139
Unemployment Insurance Act received a resolution from the Alberta Association of Registered Nurses, which reads:
-Resolved that the Alberta Association of Registered Nurses representing approximately 10,000 graduate professional nurses in the province of Alberta do strenuously object to any changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act or regulations made thereunder that would have the effect of compelling graduate professional nurses to make compulsory contributions to the unemployment insurance fund.
I did not hear the minister say whether nurses are exempted, but their profession also is one in which there is no unemployment, and it would be very unfair if they had to pay into the unemployment insurance fund all the time and not get any benefit from it. I hope the minister will tell me exactly where the nurses stand, and I hope it is in the same place as the members of the teaching profession.
It seems that for some people the Unemployment Insurance Act works out very nicely, while for others it does not work so well. About ten days ago I received a letter from a lady in my constiuency, who was laid off work last fall. She lives in a small town. Incidentally in Alberta we are not faced with the difficulty of having any local unemployment insurance offices closed because we just do not have any. These offices are in Edmonton, Calgary, and perhaps in the other bigger cities. There are none in the smaller towns, even though many of the smaller towns serve large communities.
This lady informed me that on January 21 she received a letter inquiring if she would travel more than 15 miles to work, if work were found for her. She said that during the winter she felt she should not be asked to travel more than 15 miles to find work. Later on she telephoned the office in Edmonton and told the officials she would travel a matter of 25 or 30 miles, provided it was on a good road. She immediately got word back that she had been disqualified and would not receive any more benefits.
I wrote back immediately and told her she had better make an appeal to the board of referees. She did just that, but in the meantime she is not getting any unemployment insurance benefit, and she cannot get her job back until springtime. Even though it appears to be springtime in Alberta at the moment, it is just too soon for it, and so she will have her job back probably in May. However, in the meantime she has nothing to live on.
She also told me that other people who had been working in the same place, who worked
February 29, 1968

Unemployment Insurance Act exactly the same amount of time, and who are living in the same town as she is, have not been cut off. No inquiries have been made about them and she simply cannot understand why in the world she was discriminated against. I did not bother the minister by writing to him about the case. However, I did write direct to the manager of the unemployment insurance office in Edmonton, a day or two after I had replied to the lady, and he wrote back that she had already followed my advice, that she had appealed to the board of referees, and that her file had gone to Winnipeg and was now out of his hands.
I have not yet received a reply from the Winnipeg office, but it seems very strange that people living in the same town, who had been working at the same job, who had put in exactly the same amount of time, even to the hour, were not questioned, while this one account was looked up and payment stopped. Why in the world does this procedure not apply to everybody? I think that is the way it should be.

Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the minister's remarks in closing the debate on second reading, when he referred to the problem concerning the closing of the unemployment insurance offices. This problem has been raised by nearly every member who has spoken.

In his explanation the minister mentioned two or three points, one of which was that he did not have control over this matter because it is a matter which comes under the jurisdiction of the commission, only one member of which is a government appointee, the other two being labour and management appointees. I do not think it is necessarily a bad situation to have the appointments made in this manner. It has worked in this way for a long time.
Second, he mentioned that it had relation to the computerization and the I.B.M. cards. He pointed out that it is cheaper to handle the situation in this manner. But if a service is not provided to the people, then there is no value in its being cheaper. We are trying to serve the people. We are operating an insurance plan for the workers of Canada; it is their money we are administering.
The operation of this plan should be carried out so that the needs of the people are met. I can assure the minister that there is no benefit in terms of service to the people in many of the semi-rural areas. The minister may not be aware of this but, for instance in my area, there are many people who have a limited education in the language they use. The native tongue of many people in my area is French, yet most of them attended English speaking schools. They have great difficulty understanding the forms which are provided. One question with which they have difficulty is that pertaining to transportation. They are asked whether they have transportation. In many cases the person writes "no". When I discuss the situation with such a person and have the letter from the Unemployment Insurance Commission in front of me I ask him whether he drives a car, and he answers that he does. Then I ask him whether he has a car and he states that he has. Then I say to him, "You have transportation". He replies, "No; don't have transportation". Then I ask him what he considers to be transportation and he replies, "train and bus".
This is not the fault of the person involved. If he were able to go to the unemployment insurance office they would be able to ascertain in a moment whether or not he had transportation. This, however, cannot be done by means of a computer. The computer is not able to ascertain the interpretation the applicant places on the word "transportation". There is no advantage in the computer system if it does not provide a service. That system is satisfactory when used by a large insurance company, because such a company

also has people who visit the policyholders and have a personal contact with them. It is all right for the head office to be computerized. If the post offices or the manpower centres were permitted to provide the services which formerly were provided by the unemployment insurance offices, we might be able to solve some of these problems. Originally these two important offices had a dual function, but they have now been separated.
I believe the minister must give further consideration to this matter of the division of these services. He mentioned that this came about before the last cabinet shuffle. Almost every member who has spoken has expressed his concern about the problem of non-service to the individual and the fact that the individual does not receive any satisfaction from a computer. The computer does not do anything for him; it does not give him any money either. It may satisfy the officials in the department, but it certainly does not satisfy the people. I am surprised that the Liberal members in this house have no problems. I am surprised that they appear to come from urban areas in which there are unemployment insurance offices and manpower centres in the same town.
I am not suggesting that there should be an unemployment insurance office in every town, but I am suggesting that there should be one in every area. In the future it may be necessary for a person to go to Toronto. Mr. Chairman, my remarks are not prompted by the remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming, because I intended to say something about amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. No one questions that this legislation introduced by the Liberal government has provided benefits to the Canadian working force. Over the years there have been problems. When in the

Unemployment Insurance Act absence of the Minister of Labour the Minister of National Health and Welfare introduced this bill, I was encouraged by his explanation of the unemployment insurance program the government intended to carry out, and I was particularly impressed by the action suggested in respect of abuses.
In some respects the Unemployment Insurance Act is misnamed. Most hon. members of this house have life insurance, automobile insurance, accident insurance and fire insurance. They carry this insurance, not with the certainty but with the probability of receiving benefits. When the Unemployment Insurance Act was introduced there was a great deal of unemployment in this country. It was introduced in an attempt to provide funds to support the unemployed. Since that time our standards of education and living have increased considerably.
A close look should be taken not only at this act but at other legislation of this type on our statute books. The benefits provided under various statutes should be co-ordinated. I had occasion to speak about unemployment insurance in this house not long ago, when we were considering a private member's bill. I noted that members of the official opposition asked why the government did not adopt the recommendations of the Gill committee report. Let me say that I disagree entirely with one of the recommendations of that commttee regarding the universality of unemployment insurance. The recommendation was that regardless of the probability or possibility of an individual benefiting from unemployment insurance, he should make payments in order to provide funds for others who may benefit.
The Minister of Labour denied that there was some concern among professionals and self-employed indivduals regarding payments to the unemployment insurance fund, without the likelihood of their receiving any benefits. I have received many letters in this regard from these people expressing some concern. I disagree entirely with the principle involved in this recommendation regarding universality.
I am in full support of the higher ceiling in respect of unemployment insurance payments. Wages and standards of living have increased since this bill was last amended, and I believe that the maximum allowance for a working man with dependants is hopelessly inadequate. I am happy that the maximum has not reached that proposed last summer, because I felt at the time the suggested maximum was too high.

Some members, including the hon. member for Timiskaming, have referred to problems connected with consolidation of the activities of unemployment insurance offices. I represent a riding in which the unemployment insurance office has been consolidated with the office of a neighbouring riding, so I am aware of some problems resulting from this consolidation. While I support efficiency in any government operation, the use of I.B.M. methods has created problems. Many of those seeking benefits in this country have come from foreign lands and find difficulty in filling out forms. For this reason there is some merit in the suggestion that the operations of the Unemployment Insurance Commission should be co-ordinated with those of the manpower department. In this way some direct help could be given to those individuals who are legitimately eligible for unemployment insurance benefits, but who for various reasons have difficulty filling out these forms. Many of them fill out forms inaccurately, with the result that the forms are then returned to be filled out again. This causes delays.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
There is another problem I should like to bring to the minister's attention. It has been suggested to me that in some of the larger municipalities there is a problem with regard to welfare benefits paid by the municipality. In these areas people are sometimes out of work because of specific conditions in the municipality. We all know that the municipality has the responsibility to look after people who for reasons beyond their control are not able to find an immediate means of livelihood. There is here a problem caused by the remote nature of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and it is very difficult to determine whether unemployment insurance benets are legitimately claimed and whether they should be provided. This has caused a great deal of trouble to the welfare departments in these municipalities. They do not know whether to provide sustenance immediately, whether to wait until the unemployment insurance benefits are received, or what to do about the problem.
Under the old operation-and again I say I would defend any change which reduced cost and produced more efficiency in any government operation-there was more direct liaison between the unemployment insurance office or the manpower office and the municipal welfare department. It was much easier to determine whether the unemployment insurance benefits should be paid, or whether the
February 29, 1968

responsibility should be borne immediately by the municipal welfare department, so as to make sure that people who through no fault of their own were in need of assistance were not deprived of the necessities of housing and food.
I ask the minister whether this problem has been brought to his attention by municipalities and provincial welfare departments. If there are situations where a curtailment of industrial operation due to certain circumstances has brought an increase in welfare benefits, the knowledge that individuals who apply for such assistance will receive unemployment insurance benefits, and when they will receive them, would be very important to those responsible for seeing that these people are able to provide their immediate necessities.
We know that if an individual who is eligible for unemployment insurance benefit also receives municipal welfare, it is extremely doubtful that he will return that benefit to which he is not entitled. I trust that the minister will give this matter serious consideration and will take it up with the municipalities. We have to consider that a person out of work, who is claiming unemployment insurance benefits which are not given to him when he thinks he is entitled to them, is already short of money to travel, and he runs the risk of losing his appeal. Expenses are always high in such cases, and he thereby deprives his whole family of several dollars that could be used for their needs. This puts the employee or the claimant in a difficult situation. In that connection, Mr. Chairman, I will point out that nearly every month, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, through the Unemployment Insurance Commission, discloses the number of unemployed in Canada and in each province. Sometimes we are told that there are 280,000 unemployed. Other times, there are 300,000, 400,000; I think that there are now 465,000, if not more.
I wonder whether these figures give us a true picture of the employment situation in Canada. The public is brought to believe that there are now 465,000 unemployed in Canada, but there is one thing I want to emphasize: among these 465,000 unemployed, some were working a month ago or will be working in one, two, four weeks or more. What I want to say is that during the twelve months of a year, there are a lot more than 465,000 people who, at a given time, are unemployed and apply for unemployment insurance benefits.
On June 8, 1964, the government gave me an answer to a question I had put in the

coverage, but the problems that have arisen are under constant study. The commission assures me that it will listen sympathetically to reasonable suggestions for improvement which might come from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture or from any other interested body.
