Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes at my disposal, I should like to reply to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) and tell her, first of all, that the government obviously does not have absolute jurisdiction in the field of price control.

With respect to prices it is well known that the federal jurisdiction is limited in this area. Since the federal government does not have authority to impose pervasive price controls, except in a national emergency such as war, legislation which establishes price levels is provincial legislation, and I think that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) knows this pretty well. The only exception to this in the federal field is the

DEBATES	February 29, 1968
rates set for certain public utilities, such as railway rates.
The movement of prices depends on a number of complicated factors. Some of the factors depend on world economic conditions; others relate to domestic fiscal, monetary and tariff policy. The conditions and economic expectations of the marketplace also come into play. As hon. members are aware, the department does not have responsibility for the major instruments of fiscal policy which influence the general level of prices. These matters have been dealt with on a number of occasions by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), and he has clearly shown that there is no simple solution.
Our department does have responsibility for legislation that indirectly influences the level of prices, and it is our intention as effectively as possible to use the means at our disposal. Among these means there is the Combines Investigation Act, which seeks to eliminate certain practices in restraint of trade in goods and some specific services. Under this legislation a formal inquiry into price increases is made if the price increases appear to be the result of some action which is itself an offence under that act, such as a conspiracy, an abuse of monopoly power, or an attempt to enforce resale price maintenance.
It is our intention moreover to seek to have the legislation amended to include services not presently covered by it. These amendments will have to wait until the Economic Council of Canada makes its report advising on the modernization of the Combines Investigation Act, which will make this act even more effective.
The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs can also examine and analyse selected areas of federal activities which can influence prices, and take remedial action. There is now before the house legislation to amend the Patent Act and the Trade Marks Act, which is intended to stimulate price competition among sellers of patented and trade marked drugs, through reducing protection against imports which is provided by the present legislation. When taking part in the debate the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway praised the government for bringing this important legislation before the house. This legislation is only one step in a program intended to lower the prices of drugs, while ensuring safe drugs and a viable domestic drug industry.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE-SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING REPRESENTATION BY COUNSEL
CRIMINAL CODE-SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING REPRESENTATION BY COUNSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions I have asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau) whether he is considering including a section in the omnibus bill amending the Criminal Code which would spell out the right to counsel of any person involved in difficulties with the law. I am sorry that the minister is not present tonight because, knowing his long and active interest in the question of civil liberties before he became a member of this house, I would like to get an explanation from him for his rejection of the suggestion that such a provision be added to the proposed amendments to the Criminal Code.
There is no question, Mr. Speaker, but that there have been, and frequently are cases of people who have been and are treated much more roughly by the courts than they ought to be, simply because they have not been able to afford to be represented by counsel. Several weeks ago newspapers across Canada carried reports such as this one which appeared in the Toronto Star of February 10:
The Supreme Court of Canada struck a blow for common sense and humanity this week when it ordered the release of John Hadden.
John Hadden is the British Columbia man who was sentenced to what amounts to life imprisonment for the theft of a $1.25 can opener.
He was convicted as a habitual criminal. I am certain that he, like 95 per cent of others who are convicted of being habitual criminals, was not represented by a lawyer when so charged. Similarly there was a recent case in the Quebec courts of a man accused of murder, I, believe, who testified that when he was picked up by the police, was being questioned and asked to be represented by counsel, he was refused this request. While he was being held by the police he was beaten into unconsciousness-so many times in fact that he confessed to the crime which he claims he did not commit. He may or may not have been telling the truth. The fact is, however, that he did not have counsel. I believe he should have had the right to have counsel.
I should like to remind hon. members of the Steven Truscott case. I wish to refer only
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion to the fact that Steven Truscott, a 14 year old boy, was picked up by the police and questioned for five or six hours-this fact has not been disproved by anyone-without having a lawyer represent him. When his father came to the police station to be with him the police kept his father in an anteroom. I believe this is the type of action we should not tolerate in this country. Many Canadians believe that the United States is much less a democratic country than ours, but the United States supreme court has spelled out clearly and definitely the rights of people who are being questioned by the police to be represented by counsel. To summarize a few things the supreme court said, I shall quote from an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of November 26, 1966:
The rules laid down by the U.S. Supreme Court in a series of cases this year go much farther.
This has reference to the case to which I referred.
The police must not only warn the prisoner that he is not obliged to make any statement; they must also tell him that he is entitled to counsel, and inform him of any legal aid arrangements by which he can obtain the services of a lawyer if he is unable to pay for one.
The prisoner is entitled to have his lawyer present during any questioning.
If the prisoner "indicates in any manner" that he does not wish to be interrogated, the police must stop questioning him.
If a prisoner who does not have legal assistance makes a statement to the police, this cannot be used against him at his trial unless prosecution proves that he "knowingly and intelligently" waived his legal rights.
I cannot argue with the Minister of Justice when he says that the best way to guarantee to a person the right to counsel would be to entrench that right in the charter of human rights the minister has proposed. It is obvious that in the near future some provincial governments will not give the people of Canada this kind of protection.
It seems to me there is a very simple way in which many of the things which have happened in the few illustrations I have given could be avoided, if the minister would agree to a very simple addition to his omnibus bill to amend the Criminal Code. This bill has had wonderful support, partly deserved and I believe partly undeserved, from the public. He could simply add a clause, which would state that every person who has difficulty with the police or with the law has a right to be represented by counsel.

Both the minister and I recognize the soundness of the argument which was accepted by the supreme court of the United States in the Escobedo case. The minister has illustrated his acceptance by the proposed Canadian charter for human rights which, not very many weeks ago, he proposed to be accepted by the provincial attorneys general and the heads of government of various provinces.
In regard to the answer given at that time I can add nothing more except perhaps to repeat what he said at that time, that the problem of individual liberty as it may be challenged by action in the courts is not confined to the Criminal Code, but extends throughout a much broader field. Some of the celebrated cases in the courts in recent years have not been under the Criminal Code, but under provincial jurisdiction, as in cases of mental incompetency applications. I am aware that the hon. member is aware of those cases. I find no lis or disagreement between myself and the hon. member on the desirability of this kind of change in the laws of our country.
The main question is how best to effect a change. I share the minister's viewpoint that ultimately and fundamentally this can best be affected by the kind of change in our basic law on human rights which he has proposed by the basic entrenched right to counsel before the courts.

maintopic: INDUSTRY-POSSIBLE CHANGE IN CRITERIA RESPECTING DESIGNATED AREAS
INDUSTRY-POSSIBLE CHANGE IN CRITERIA RESPECTING DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the criteria established by the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) in relation to areas which may become designated for assistance for the development and economic growth of primary industry are such that they may be helpful. Obviously they have been helpful in some areas because there are some 80 areas designated. However, this militates against certain other areas, because the program does not take into account in alternative criteria the factors of seasonality in certain industries.
[Mr. Orlikow.l
In British Columbia the logging and sawmill industries are primarily seasonal, as is the construction, fishing and other industries. They are affected by the seasons. Because of seasonality, people find themselves out of work on a regular basis. There is no seasona-bility factor taken into account in the criteria established for the designation of areas needing development.
It may very well be that the income derived by individuals employed in these seasonal occupations at times will be higher than the $4,250 set out as the floor under the area development criteria for designated areas. The fact is that the seasonality of this situation and the regular occurrence of unemployment tend to depress the economy of a whole area. For argument's sake let us consider the logging industry in British Columbia. In that industry there is a regular period of unemployment, and there are regular depressed periods during specific times throughout the years which should be taken into account.
I ask that this situation be looked at very carefully. I have no suggestion to make at this time about the words which might be used to spell out the matter of seasonability or seasonality of employment, but it is a fact that should be included in the criteria. If it is included, it will mean that those areas which now find themselves in an awkward position, unable to fit into the criteria, unable to receive the assistance provided by the area development program, will be able to receive such assistance and the level of economic activity and the well-being of the people, which is the prime concern of the program, will be improved.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry
maintopic: INDUSTRY-POSSIBLE CHANGE IN CRITERIA RESPECTING DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of seasonality is one that I think can justly be said to be of concern in the administration of the area development program, and has been so from the inception of the program. As the house may well be aware, there was originally in the criteria employed for the designation of areas to benefit under the area development program this factor of seasonality which, in the instance given by the hon. member, is a matter of such concern.
Curiously, or perhaps not curiously but naturally, because of the wide variety of economic activity in this country and the wide variety of occupations, early criteria founded on the basis of seasonality were the subject of very considerable debate and very considerable criticism. The critics maintained that the
February 29, 1968

criteria unduly favoured certain areas which did not really fall within the basic purpose of the program, which is to assist areas of chronic unemployment or underemployment of the labour force.
Hon. members may recall that the employment seasonality which was the subject of so much comment was in areas with industries of relatively high levels of employment and relatively high pay levels, such as the automobile industry and the farm machinery industry where areas were designated and which in fact, when applying broader judgment to the question, did not really seem to be areas of chronic underemployment or unemployment.
It was as a result of comments of this nature and a broader judgment of the program within this context that the seasonal factor was removed, and in the criteria to be used by the area development program it was decided to try to arrive at some kind of averaging throughout the entire year's employment to find out if, in fact, taking the year as
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion a whole, there really was a chronic area of unemployment or underemployment of the labour force such as to require the special incentives that the program provides.
I regret that I cannot assure the hon. member that the change he proposes will automatically become a change of law. I can assure him that, as has been the case in each of the years the program has been in effect, the statistics employed for the purpose of establishing the designation of particular areas will be reviewed annually. I would remind the house that as a result of this annual review the criteria have been changed from time to time. I am confident that in the course of the review of the statistics which will take place in the coming year, once again the question of the problem of seasonality as related to chronic unemployment will be considered, and not any the less because of the representations made by the hon. member.
